title: Effect of menstrual cycle phase on physiological and perceptual responses during complex contrast training
summary:
Background
Women’s bodies go through regular changes during the menstrual cycle, e.g., changes in hormone levels. These hormones may influence how the muscles and the nervous system work, how tired they become during exercise, how quickly they recover, and how difficult exercise feels. Studies so far have produced mixed results. One reason is that the menstrual cycle phase was often not checked reliably. Very little is known about demanding strength and power training in women, in which heavy lifts are alternated with fast, explosive jumps and movements.

Question
Does the menstrual cycle phase influence how fatigued the neuromuscular system becomes after a complex contrast training session, how quickly it recovers over the following 24 hours, and how women feel during and after the session (for example, perceived effort, muscle soreness and menstrual symptoms)?

Methodology
In total, thirty healthy women aged 18 to 35 years will be recruited. The participants have a natural, regular menstrual cycle, and previous experience in strength training. The participants do not use hormonal birth control.  Each woman completes eight visits at the university laboratory over about two menstrual cycles. In the first visit she is informed and the requirements are checked. In the second visit she learns all the tests and her maximal strength levels are tested. In the following three visits she performs the same complex contrast training session, once in each of three phases of her cycle: at the beginning of the cycle, shortly before ovulation, and about one week after ovulation. The order of the phases is determined by chance and differs between participants. Each training session is followed by a short recovery visit the next morning. Muscle strength, jump height, and how well the nervous system can activate the muscles are assessed before, during and for four hours after each session, and again the next morning after approximately 24 hours. We also record muscle activity with sensors on the skin, heart rate and its recovery, breathing gases, and venous blood samples from the arm, the fingertip and the earlobe. Women complete questionnaires on how recovered and stressed they feel and on their menstrual symptoms. The menstrual cycle is tracked with a calendar and ovulation test strips, and a blood test before each session is used afterwards to check hormone levels and to confirm that each session took place in the intended phase. Every woman is compared with herself across the three phases.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Eumenorrheic menstrual cycle
- Minimum 12 months of resistance training experience
- Minimum training frequency of two sessions per week
- Relative strength level at least one times body weight in Smith-machine back squat
Exclusion criteria:
- BMI <18.5 or >30 kg/m²
- Hormonal contraceptive use
- Pregnancy
- Fertility treatment
- Cardiovascular, pulmonary, metabolic, or other relevant diseases
- Recent illness or infection in the last 2 weeks
- Musculoskeletal injury within the previous 6 months
- Daily smoking
- Medication affecting hormonal, cardiovascular, metabolic, or neuromuscular function
- Menstrual cycle abnormalities (e.g., amenorrhea, oligomenorrhea, PCOS, endometriosis, PMDD)
- Low energy availability
- Conditions affecting hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis function
